p.x:
Last month someone asked for recommendations of female jhana teachers. I've mostly gravitated towards male teachers across the lineages I've participated/participate in. Some archetypal resonance of the positive embodiment I aspire to emulate perhaps accounts for it, as well as what seems a general gender-disparity in the teachers that are available. Regardless of the reason, for longer-term mentorship especially, it's important to find a teacher/teachers who you can connect with.

These are some of the female teachers I know and/or have heard from those I trust are excellent. Please add other recommendations below. My knowledge and network are far from complete!

For jhana/Theravada and Theravada-influenced more broadly:

Leigh Brasington has recommended Mary Aubry, for whom I didn't find contact info but you may be able to (https://t.co/BUVHW6uJzy), and Rachel O'Brien (https://t.co/0AWHgKiApQ).

In Pa-Auk's lineage there's Tina Rasmussen, (https://t.co/Usnf0rSE6E), Beth Upton (https://t.co/nQ6X8ilIW5), Shaila Catherine (https://t.co/YNNfdnE3W5), and Nikki Mirghafori (https://t.co/X8CzScA51G).

For Zen, I worked 1:1 with Hojin Sensei at ZMM during sesshin a fair bit, and she's in Brooklyn most of the time, (https://t.co/hcgFidGFEd), there's Hidden Valley Zen Center with Sozui Roshi (https://t.co/kLOSSIc5iN), and Cristina Moon at Chozen-ji, (https://t.co/00iZjit8hE).

For Vajrayana and Dzogchen, Lama Lena (https://t.co/cvXqbD6aL7), Anne Klein (https://t.co/cvXqbD6aL7), and @_awbery_ of course on the experimental, non-binary/nondual end.

Cheers!

In this video I try to circle around something that is very difficult to speak about directly — the void.
From the opening verses of Genesis, where the earth is described as “empty and void,” we are confronted with a mystery that runs through Scripture, philosophy, and our own experience. What is the “not that” which underlies being? Why has the modern world become so fascinated with negativity, difference, and alterity? And how do we understand the necessary — yet possibly dangerous — role of emptiness in the structure of reality?

JP takes a necessary risk and lands it.

Highest recommendation.

The rules of professional product development are being rewritten in real time. 

- PMs and designers can ship software as easily as engineers.
- Software is no longer just built for humans—it’s also built for agents as first-class citizens. 

To better understand how we build products in this world, I invited Mike Krieger (@mikeyk) on @every’s AI & I podcast. Mike cofounded Instagram and is now a member of the technical staff at Anthropic, co-leading Anthropic Labs, their internal incubator for experimental products. He's been at the frontier of two transformative technology waves: mobile/social and now agent-native software.

We discussed: 
- How to build a truly agent-native product. The best products today, like Claude Code, allow users to do things that their creators never intended. But that requires hard trade-offs between freedom and safety/reliability for frontier products, an issue that Mike's team is learning how to solve. 
- What's different about building now versus building Instagram. At Instagram, it took months to hit dead ends and learn what to cut. Now, that cycle runs in hours.
- The trap of building too much, too fast with agents. You can go from idea to a nearly-shipped product in a day, but that process doesn’t give you the incremental feedback that used to tell you what not to build. The models are great at adding features, but can create a product that lacks coherence.
- How Anthropic Labs structures product teams. New product experiments are led by only two people, usually a product manager or designer paired with an engineer. Mike says bigger teams tend to be too slow because of coordination costs.
- Why you need to throw out your product and start over every three to six months. AI progress means most of your harness will be outdated quickly—the best teams build this into their product strategy.

And much more! You should watch this one.
